content: Cleaning and disinfection of surfaces and equipment between patients is a standard practice to prevent cross-contamination. This is strongly recommended, although the evidence comparing the effectiveness of disposable versus reusable aprons is of very low quality. Protective body wear, such as gowns or coveralls, is advised as part of contact precautions, particularly in the context of filovirus diseases like Ebola. Both gowns and coveralls are considered equally acceptable, as there is no definitive evidence to suggest that one is more effective than the other in reducing transmission to healthcare workers. Gowns are generally easier to don and doff, making them a safer option during the removal of personal protective equipment (PPE). They are also more familiar to healthcare workers, which increases the likelihood of their correct use and removal. This familiarity facilitates training and reduces the risk of errors. Additionally, gowns cause significantly less heat stress compared to coveralls and are more readily available in regions affected by filovirus outbreaks. In some cultural contexts, gowns may also be more acceptable for use by women. Fluid-resistant protective body wear is recommended to prevent the penetration of infected body fluids, which could contaminate underlying clothing or skin and lead to unrecognized transmission via contact with mucous membranes of the eyes, nose, or mouth. An apron should be worn over the gown or coveralls, as it is easier to remove a soiled apron than a soiled gown or coverall. Aprons are typically worn for the entire duration of a healthcare worker's time in the treatment area. If an apron becomes visibly soiled, it should be removed and replaced with a disposable one. Feasibility issues, such as the availability of new aprons and waste disposal within isolation areas, must be addressed. Healthcare workers using reusable aprons should leave the ward to clean, disinfect, and remove the apron. Waterproof boots are preferred over closed shoes for healthcare workers caring for patients with filovirus diseases. Boots are easier to clean and disinfect and provide optimal protection when floors are wet. Rubber boots also offer protection against sharp injuries. If boots are unavailable, closed shoes that fully cover the dorsum of the foot and ankles should be worn, ideally with non-slip, impermeable shoe covers to facilitate decontamination. Boots do not need to be removed upon leaving the PPE removal area, provided they have been cleaned and disinfected. The same pair of boots can be worn until the end of the workday or shift. All healthcare workers should wear a head cover that protects the head and neck while providing clinical care for patients with filovirus diseases. This is to prevent virus exposure. The head cover should ideally be separate from the gown or coverall to allow for independent removal. The purpose of head covers is to protect the skin and hair from contamination and prevent subsequent unrecognized transmission to mucosal surfaces. Hair and hair extensions must fit inside the head cover. If a separate head cover is unavailable, a coverall with a hood can be used, provided the hood is donned after eye, nose, and mouth protection to maintain mucosal protection during removal. Light-colored PPE is preferred to better detect possible contamination. Thumb or finger loops can help anchor sleeves in place. PPE materials should meet specific standards for resistance to blood and body fluid penetration, such as ISO 16603 or ISO 16604, depending on the level of protection required. Materials associated with higher heat stress and reduced breathability, such as those described in ISO 16604, may require more frequent changes and shorter continuous wear times. Surgical scrubs, consisting of trousers and a top, are recommended as regular on-duty wear but are not considered PPE. Scrubs are preferable to street clothes for healthcare workers on duty. They should be tightly woven, minimize linting, and be available in reusable or single-use options. Tops should have short sleeves, and trousers should have a drawstring waist. Different sizes should be available to ensure proper fit. The development of these guidelines involved a systematic review of the literature, expert consultation, and consideration of the biology and transmission modes of the virus. Filovirus infections are primarily transmitted through contact with infected blood or body fluids, such as vomit, feces, sweat, saliva, urine, amniotic fluid, and semen. The virus is most concentrated in blood, although bleeding occurs in only a minority of patients. Transmission occurs through mucous membrane contact (mouth, nose, eyes) or non-intact skin, such as through needle-stick injuries. Intact skin has not been documented as a route of transmission. Hand hygiene and gloves are essential to protect healthcare workers and prevent transmission to others. Face covers, protective footwear, gowns or coveralls, and head covers are also critical components of PPE to prevent transmission. The selection of PPE aims to balance optimal protection against filovirus infection with the ability to provide patient care effectively, ensuring ease of use, comfort, and minimal heat-associated stress. Heat stress is a significant concern with impermeable PPE, as it increases the risk of accidental exposure to the virus. Comprehensive training and mentoring on PPE use are fundamental to preventing filovirus disease among healthcare workers.
